A hash table is a way to store key–value pairs so that, most of the time, you can retrieve the value attached to a key without scanning every stored item. Its central idea is to turn the key itself into an address. The table keeps an array of buckets, and a hash function converts a key such as a name or an identification number into an integer. That integer is then reduced, usually by taking its remainder modulo the number of buckets, to produce a bucket index within the array. If an entry is stored in that bucket, looking it up begins at the same place. To find a value, the table hashes the key in the same way, goes to the indicated bucket, and examines the entries there. If the key matches, the associated value is returned. The appeal is that hashing skips the search over all entries and starts close to the answer.

A useful hash function is deterministic, quick to compute, and good at spreading different keys across the bucket array. It need not produce a unique number for every key; it only needs to make different keys land in many different buckets most of the time. This matters because the bucket array is finite. Many possible keys must share a limited set of bucket positions, so collisions are inevitable in ordinary use. A collision simply means that two distinct keys receive the same bucket index. The table must still be able to tell the entries apart and find the right one, which is why the stored key itself, not just its hash, remains part of the entry.

Chaining handles collisions by giving each bucket a place to hold more than one entry. A bucket might contain a short linked list, or a small dynamic collection, of key–value records. Each record holds the full key, the value, and a link or reference to the next record in the same bucket. When a new key collides with an existing one, it is added to that bucket's chain. During a lookup, the hash calculation identifies the bucket, and then the chain in that bucket is searched record by record. For each record, the stored key is compared with the key being sought. If they match, the value is returned; if not, the search continues along the chain. If it reaches the end without a match, the key is absent. This comparison step is essential, since two different keys can share a bucket index.

As entries accumulate, chains can get longer, and longer chains mean more comparisons. The load factor gives a compact way to monitor this pressure. It is the number of stored entries divided by the number of buckets. A table with ten entries and twenty buckets has a load factor of one half; a table with nineteen entries and twenty buckets has a load factor close to one. When the load factor rises above a chosen threshold, the table resizes. It allocates a larger bucket array, usually around twice the old size, and rehashes every existing key into the new array. Rehashing means recomputing each key's bucket index using the new bucket count and moving the entry accordingly. Resizing is relatively expensive, because it touches every existing entry, but it happens only occasionally. Spread over many insertions, its cost is typically amortized, while the larger array keeps chains short and lookups fast.

The familiar claim that hash-table lookup is constant time is an expected or average-case claim, not a guarantee for every possible set of keys. Under the assumptions that the hash function spreads keys roughly uniformly, the load factor is kept under control, and key comparisons take constant time, a lookup examines a bucket plus a short chain whose expected length is a small constant. That is why the usual expectation is constant time, written as order one: doubling the number of entries normally does not double the work of finding one key. The worst case is different. If every key happens to land in the same bucket, perhaps because of a poor hash function or deliberately chosen colliding keys, that bucket's chain contains every entry. A lookup then becomes a linear search through the chain, taking time proportional to the number of entries. With chaining, the worst case is therefore linear, even though the ordinary case is expected to be constant. The distinction comes from probability and distribution, not from an absolute promise.

A small made-up example can make the mechanics concrete. Suppose a tiny table has four buckets, numbered zero through three, and the keys cedar, maple, and pine are to be stored. For illustration only, imagine a hash function that assigns cedar to bucket one, maple to bucket three, and pine to bucket one. These assignments are invented for the example and are not meant to describe any real hash function. Inserting cedar places its record in bucket one. Inserting maple places its record in bucket three, where it is alone. Inserting pine sends it to bucket one as well, so pine is added to cedar's chain there. Looking up maple recomputes its bucket as three, finds the matching record immediately, and returns maple's value. Looking up pine recomputes bucket one, walks the chain, compares pine with cedar and finds they are different, then compares pine with pine and returns the value. If more keys arrived and the load factor crossed its threshold, the table would resize and rehash; cedar and pine might then be separated. The lookup still follows the same basic route: hash the key, choose the bucket, compare along the chain.

That is how the lookup finds its way.
